prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made possible atomic frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for optical lattice clocks (B052) to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The discovery is a specific physical idea, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength where the light shift cancels between the clock levels, so that thousands of atoms are interrogated Doppler-free and recoil-free. That idea was then taken by independent laboratories to the 10^-18 level, with agreement between clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Braunschweig, Paris and elsewhere, and with a controlled treatment of the many-body effects that appear once atoms are packed in a lattice. This is the opposite of a result that waits for a single laboratory to be believed. After reading the full first-round exchange I note, with the chair, that seven of eight configurations converge on B052 and that some of this convergence came from reading each other, myself included, so I do not count the support as evidence. My support rests on three things I can judge as a quantum physicist: the regime is new (many-atom interrogation of a forbidden optical transition at the quantum-limited level), the result is verified quantitatively across laboratories, and the credit divides into two roles that can be written in a sentence. Katori proposed the scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group brought it to record systematic uncertainty and coherence and showed what happens in a degenerate, interacting lattice gas. I propose that the citation name the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, so that it neither repeats the 2005 frequency-comb prize nor anticipates any later recognition of a nuclear clock.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real and I do not think they are only drafting matters. First, Olsson's attribution concern about Ye: if the committee cannot point to Ye's own original steps, the prize would be recognising an improvement of Katori's invention, and a Katori-led or differently composed citation would be more defensible. I think the record supports Ye, but I am relying on memory of priority and have not re-verified dates. Second, Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Lisdat at PTB, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg lattice groups all made real contributions that a two-name list leaves outside, and the ion-clock community (Al+ and others) will see the same narrative credited elsewhere. Third, the fundamental-physics reach, constants, dark matter and relativistic geodesy, is demonstrated in proof-of-principle form and is mostly prospective, so the case is strongest as a discovery of a measurement regime, not of new physics. Fourth, B052 is a third prize in the precision-spectroscopy line (2005, 2012), and that may be read as precedent-driven even though I argue it should not be.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's contribution is an original and decisive step or an improvement of Katori's invention, and says that a Katori-only or differently composed citation would be more defensible if the committee cannot show Ye's own original contributions.
responses.response: This is the question the chair put to me and I will answer it as concretely as I can from the physics, with the caveat that dates are from memory. Katori's contribution is the magic-wavelength proposal and the first Sr lattice clock. Ye's group contributions are not merely a better version of the same device. They include the demonstration of very long coherence on the clock transition in a lattice, the evaluation of density- and collision-related shifts, the observation of many-body (Fermi-degenerate, spin-exchange) physics in the clock, and the push to systematic uncertainty near 10^-18 that is the number the whole field now quotes. The last of these is not a refinement but what turned the proposal into a regime of measurement: without it, no one would have been able to compare lattice clocks at millimetre height differences. I therefore regard Ye as a co-originator of the lattice clock as a working instrument, whereas Katori is the originator of its principle. If the committee prefers a stricter reading of 'original experiment', I would accept a citation that stresses the magic-wavelength lattice, but I would not drop Ye, because a Katori-only prize would not describe why the lattice clock matters physically.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B024), argues that flat-band correlated phases exist regardless of how the pairing question is resolved, and lists B052 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept your point that the existence of the correlated insulator and flat-band phenomena is robust and does not depend on the pairing mechanism, and I withdraw any suggestion that the pairing question by itself makes B024 premature. My remaining objection is about credit, not maturity. The three names you propose leave out Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers and the earlier band-theory work, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald result is one paper credited to two of the three places. The Katori and Ye split follows two distinct contributions by two people with no one comparable left outside who is not a competing clock group. As a theorist I am glad you are on the committee to carry the materials judgement. I would not call B024 premature, and I expect it to return as a strong candidate. I would still not choose it this year over B052 because the attribution rule is harder to state.

responses.point: The chair observes that seven configurations on B052 should not be read as seven independent judgements, that atomic physics is outside his own expertise, and that round 2 should test the B052 case with the AMO members.
responses.response: I agree with the chair's caution and I will treat it as a request. The test I can offer, as a circuit-QED and quantum-optics person who is not an atomic clock specialist myself, is whether the case survives the two objections that would most weaken it: that it duplicates the comb and ion-trap prizes, and that Ye's role is derivative. On the first, the comb is the ruler that reads out an optical frequency, whereas the lattice clock is a decision about how to hold the atoms, and the physics that is new is the magic-wavelength cancellation and many-atom interrogation. On the second, see my reply to Olsson. I would add that the AMO members, Lindroth and Kroll, should say plainly if they find the priority record insufficient, since I defer to them on lattice-clock history and am relying on the same memory as everyone else.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B052 for its broad support, clean attribution and maturity, but notes that the fundamental-physics reach is mostly prospective and that Ye's possible later credit for the thorium nuclear clock might affect timing.
responses.response: I agree that the fundamental-physics reach is prospective, and I would not put dark matter or varying constants in the citation. On the nuclear clock, I do not think a possible later recognition of Ye for thorium-229 is a reason to wait. The lattice clock is mature now, and a later nuclear-clock prize would be a different discovery with different credited names. That is an argument for wording the citation around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping so that it is clearly separate, as we both seem to want. I also share your caution about your own B021: I think it is a very strong physics case but the credit problem you name is real, and I would not want it dropped from future consideration.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's role will be accepted by the committee as an original contribution and not an improvement of Katori's invention, which depends on priority details I have recalled from memory and not verified.

Whether the citation should be framed around magic-wavelength trapping, as I propose, or around accuracy, and whether any wording will satisfy members who see the work as a sequel to the 2005 comb prize.
How the credit of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg lattice and Al+ ion-clock groups should be handled, since a two-name prize necessarily leaves them out.

I have not changed my view that no second part is needed; atom interferometry (B035) is the natural companion but I regard its attribution without Chu as unresolved, and IceCube (B043) as a strong later candidate whose source identifications are still thin. B010 and B024 attribution I leave to colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a Chalmers MC2 theorist working on superconducting circuits, so I am close to the field of B056 (circuit QED) and to groups around it, and I would recuse myself from any decision on B056 if it became a live option. It is in no configuration and I removed it from my alternatives. I co-authored the observation of the dynamical Casimir effect with Chalmers colleagues. I note Kroll's WACQT role and the Gothenburg overlap with Mehlig and Olsson as institutional only. I have no specific conflict regarding B052, B035, B043 or the other shortlisted ballots.
